Constrained decoding has been in vLLM for a long time, and constrained tool call decoding has been in vLLM for a while, too.

The blog post is rather confusing because until you understand the entire situation it appears to imply that they fixed vLLM (what the title implies) but really they just needed to configure it correctly.

To be fair, the course of constrained tool calling configuration in vLLM changed over time in ways that changed behavior, which is the real problem. The Ubicloud team deserves a lot of credit for having benchmarks in place to track performance and catch regressions for investigations. Some of the providers you find on OpenRouter have inexplicably bad performance relative to others and clearly do not care this much.

However, if this article left you confused because constrained decoding and constrained tool call schema have been features in vLLM for a long time, jump to the end where they show what configuration changes they made.

Overall, a fair assessment. I do want to place a footnote here that we did fix vLLM in the sense that its correct behavior for Kimi required code changes: it was impossible to fix it in the configuration. Later, the vLLM team fixed this problem upstream. Now, with the latest version of vLLM, the problem we describe can be addressed by setting the `--tool-strict-level` flag to `parameter`.

Amusingly constrained decoding is the same approach we use to turn an AR model into a /v1/systemone endpoint (I worked on the vLLM feature).

Tool calling is fraught with peril, especially because there's nothing that necessarily says that a models tools are fixed in place for the life of its run. In some cases, tools are added mid-run to avoid a giant prefix miss and (at least last time I checked!), the industry has not settled on OpenAI-style chat message formats for tool call updates.

I would absolutely prefer to run in a fully-constrained tool call environment, and would love if we hadn't YOLO'd the whole thing! The PTC-style tools sort of fix this by punting tool calling to JavaScript, but that's even harder to enforce, and models not trained on the style might take a turn of failed tool calls to get it right.

> avoid a giant prefix miss

I was wondering how feasible it is to modify the context, instead of just appending - e.g. to remove malformed tool calls and their error messages that would pollute the context otherwise.

Sure, you'd have to rebuild the KV cache and take a performance loss, but that might be acceptable if it happens rarely enough.

This is the approach I took. Before leaving scope, results are filtered to remove tool call errors and bloat and instead append those errors to a different system. A much smaller tool call error result is returned to the agent while keeping the reasoning for failure intact.

>some cases, tools are added mid-run to avoid a giant prefix miss

Wait, can you actually do that? The model should not exactly care where in the context the tools are, but I haven't realised it's a thing that works

Context is just one long string. You can do whatever you want with it. Training helps to conform to specific syntactic idiosyncrasies, but LLMs are large enough these days that they can follow pretty much any instructions most of the time.

For example, if you want to use an LLM API that does not natively support tool calls, you can tell the LLM to emit the tool calls for your preferred tools in a markdown code block and parse them yourself.
What would a "fully-constrained tool call environment" be?

I wish they'd published something about the actual impact on model quality. Schema-constrained decoding changes the distribution the LLM will output. I'd be curious how a back-up-and-retry method for tool calls (which also doesn't pollute the context and also has 100% tool-call accuracy) would compare. In their example stats (23/25 success rate), it'd be +9% tokens used for the tool call attempt itself, but that's +9% on just a small fraction of the total tokens, so if a retry solution gave any better accuracy I think it might win out.

We are also interested in this and may focus on it in a future post. They are two different perspectives: (1) What is the overall quality of LLM+serving stack+harness, and (2) How close does the behavior of our setup match the first-party provider's? In this post, we focused on the latter. Moonshot AI, the creators of Kimi, recommend constrained decoding to be on by default, and also serve Kimi that way. This implies that it helps overall performance, though it does not provide numbers for it. We want to serve Kimi as recommended, and ran into the challenges described in the post.

There is work that suggests that constrained decoding can negatively affect model quality, but this depends on many factors, among which the model in question [1, 2, 3]. Overall, it seems to me that there is a trend towards using constrained decoding. OpenAI's newer Responses API has constrained decoding turned on by default as well, similar to Moonshot AI's Kimi.

2: https://blog.dottxt.ai/say-what-you-mean.html

3: https://dylancastillo.co/posts/say-what-you-mean-sometimes.h...

Is the schema constraint not implemented in a way where the new distribution is identically scaled to the old distribution with retry? I had thought the way it worked was just to disallow invalid next states... oh, or is the idea that you think it is much preferred to retry at the level of the entire tool call, rather than (conceptually) per token? I guess I can see that making a lot of sense, as maybe the model gets "backed into a corner", so to speak, with a really bad initial choice and is then trying to rescue horrible states?

The way it works is to disallow invalid next states, and getting backed into a corner is one way to think about one possible failure mode.

For a concrete example (happens less nowadays with bigger models, but it still happens, especially later into a context window), models hate long json strings. It's very easy to get a json output like

{"name": "Bob", "biography": "Bob is a fantastic builder, having ...

Critically, the ellipses terminate the JSON. With schema-constrained decoding, you _must_ eventually terminate that broken string, and it'll typically terminate it right after the ellipses. Basically, by the point you got to the first period the output was borked. You were backed into a corner. Retry as a strategy fixes that.

As another example failure mode that's a bit more subtle, you might have a set of "correct" tokens early on in the output which get the KV cache into a bit of a wonky state, causing it to have worse outputs toward the end of your output. Disallowing invalid next states forces you to generate tokens in that worse-output state. Retry lets you fail more often and then hopefully not have those wonky-state early tokens. It's not really that you were backed into a bad state as a hard rule, but that you were backed into a bad state as a probabilistic statement.

For a toy model to think about, suppose the entire grammar is [ab, ba], and the LLM's universe of training data is [ab, ab, ba, bb]. The "right" distribution (retry on failure) is {ab: 67%, ba: 33%}. The schema-constrained distribution is {ab: 50%, ba: 50%}.

What the other guy means is the model is forced to decode potentially out of distribution and subsequent parts of the sequence will be sampled from a higher-entropy distribution.

i.e. it might be that a particular model may need some additional conditioning, or perhaps adjusting the order of the json output affects it to produce lower-quality results.

You have to remember that the LLM will be expected to generate 10s of thousands of tokens on a single turn, where things like quantization noise lead to cascading error further on. So when you can, you really want to stay within the model's distribution.

> or perhaps adjusting the order of the json output affects it to produce lower-quality results.

The order of the output fields can actually be used to tune performance of the outputs. It can be helpful to force the LLM to reason about specific fields first if later fields benefit from seeing those earlier fields' output. You have to test it because some times the results are surprising in directions you didn't expect.

XGrammar has an option somewhere to allow fields to appear in any order but I don't know if vLLM exposes it. There are some tradeoffs and limitations for allowing fields to show up in any order because there is some complexity in schema parsing like that.

Technically true, but this is a very inefficient optimization strategy and usually indicates some structural issue with your setup.

When you know enough about the JSON structure to understand how to set a decoding order, then you can simply break the problem into smaller parts so it's more manageable.

Otherwise, you have these solutions: - GEPA-style prompt optimization for simple agents - If working with large models, you can just have them do step-by-step problem solving & relying on their CoT for accuracy. - A small model can simply be trained to do what you want

And if those don't work, I would be extremely surprised.

I guess to be more concrete, I thought the way schema aware decoding worked should be identical to a token-level retry: "only even dice rolls are allowed" converting {0:0.1, 1:0.2, 2:0.2, 3:0.1, 4:0.2, 5:0.2} into {0:0.2, 2:0.4, 4:0.4}. That is why I am asking if the difference being stared at is doing the retry at the level of the entire tool call rather than each token (as this let's later errors in the schema re-roll the earlier committed states)? (But like, it isn't clear to me that's what they mean, so I feel a need to ask; as an example, you are now talking about field order, but that's an entirely different issue involving an overly-constrained constraint: nothing would prevent implementing the grammar for the constrained decoding to allow the fields in any order, and if you allow duplicate fields -- which JSON typically allows anyway -- then it is probably already supported as the language loses its additional context requirement.)
Schema-constrained is equivalent to token-level retry. It's not equivalent to retry of longer sequences.

Right... and I said exactly that in both my comments, but I was looking for confirmation that that's the issue being stared at, as it wasn't obvious to me that's what was meant and (I will cite as demonstration of the confusion) now people are bringing up other ideas (such as field order, which is an entirely unrelated constraint). (FWIW, since you are the person I was originally asking, I will take this as positive confirmation that "yes: I am saying it is better to retry the entire tool call" ;P.)

Ah, I see. IMO the other response [0] I gave is probably the closest to what I had in mind. Interestingly, retry very well might not be better, especially when measured on a pareto frontier including cost.

I have a reasonably strong prior that it should be better though. That comes from my observations that whenever I notice the difference in distribution the retry method is better (obvious sampling bias, but what kind of person ignores their own experiences). As a stronger piece of evidence and intuition, the entire goal of these systems is to reproduce a certain distribution. If that distribution says that you should use ripgrep 10x as often as you should use grep then that's a signal you probably don't want to throw away. Constrained decoding might very well do so and place them on even footing or skew 10x the other direction. Retry faithfully captures that original distribution. I'm skeptical of solutions which want to shy too far away from it (similarly with most applications of changing the model's temperature).

The more important point is just that they're different, so we should probably measure the impact.

> but massaging the sampler(?) also sounds like that might give a lot of control over outputs with the weights staying technically the same?

Yes, this is what constrained decoding means. You constrain the model to only output from a set of "allowed" tokens (a.k.a. grammars).

So, if you use tool use with constrained decoding, you can be certain that the model will always choose from a list of approved tools (i.e. if tools=['read','write'], it cannot output 'execute', even if in other sessions it could, if execute was in the approved tools).

The tricky problem is that certain models work / have been trained in certain ways. And constraining them can lead to "invisible" problems. Constrained decoding only guarantees perfect syntax, not perfect semantics (i.e. it could write nonsense in the correct file).

> Could something like that also be used in other contexts?

Sure. You can build pretty cool grammars and constrain the model to do cool stuff, akin to "tool use" but more free hand. You could, for example, make it always emit a 10 point plan. For any prompt, it will give you a fixed syntax 10 point plan, always. And the plan will be constant with a plan_title and 10{plan_item, item_text}. But, as above, there's no guarantee that the individual items in the plan would make any sense... (i.e. step7 in a pasta making recipe would be "add glue").

> For example, when we served Kimi K2.6 with vLLM version 0.28, we got the expected tool call schema only 92% of the time. In other words, 2 out of every 25 attempted tool calls failed.

100% success is critical for tool calling.

The probability that the overall agent iteration is successful would scale very poorly even if we achieved 95%. With p95, if you need 50 tool calls that must execute sequentially to achieve a result, the chances that you won't have an error are only ~8%. There are ways to recover from bad tool calls (error feedback helps a lot), but if the agent is persistently using the wrong tools with the wrong args the overall system will not work very well.

Can the same mechanism be used to make sure it outputs syntactically correct code?

Yes. All you need is a formal grammar that defines the syntax of the text being generated. The llama.cpp repo has a decent writeup on the way that grammar-constrained decoding works in general [0], and it includes a bit of a simplistic example for generating syntactically-correct C code [1]. No reason this couldn't be extended to other things -- I personally have run experiments with generating syntactically-correct SQL statements when doing text-to-sql [2], and I think it's pretty cool.

Yes, absolutely. The problem is integrating it into the inference engine. Not impossible, just _very hard_.

Also less useful than one might think at first.

Lots of code "typos" aren't immediately syntactic errors. Misbalanced parentheses, for example, only bite when one needs to close the series. The solution is to go back and fix the original error, but that option is foreclosed to autoregressive LLMs. In the meantime, forcing the model off what it "wants" to generate might make the remaining syntactically valid tokens semantically meaningless, impairing future generation in a way that's hard to quntify.

Constrained generation for tool calls is certainly a type of syntax checking, but it's one that can be justified because the "hard" syntax choices come up front, both in the very format of the tool call itself to the name of the tool and its parameters. Errors are more likely to be detected in the same root-cause tokens that generate them.
